q: In benzene, each carbon atom is hybridised as:
x: Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two to C, one to H) using three sp² hybrid orbitals. The remaining unhybridised 2p orbital takes part in the delocalised π system.

q: Ethene reacts with bromine, and benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃. The organic products are, respectively:
x: Ethene adds Br₂ across its double bond to give CH₂BrCH₂Br. Benzene substitutes one hydrogen to give C₆H₅Br and HBr, keeping its aromatic ring.

q: Hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises methylbenzene to benzoic acid but leaves benzene unchanged. This shows that:
o: The ring is oxidised before the side chain
The benzene ring resists oxidation, while the alkyl side chain is oxidised
The methyl group makes the ring easier to oxidise
Benzene is more easily oxidised than alkanes
x: The stable aromatic ring survives strong oxidising agents, but the side chain attached to it is oxidised to –COOH. So methylbenzene gives C₆H₅COOH while benzene does not react.

q: The benzene ring is flat, whereas the ring in cyclohexane (C₆H₁₂) is puckered. The reason is that in benzene:
o: Each carbon is sp³ hybridised, and its 109.5° bond angles fit a flat regular hexagon
Each carbon is sp² hybridised, and its 120° bond angles fit a flat regular hexagon
Each carbon is sp hybridised, and its 180° bond angles hold the ring straight
The π electrons lie in the plane of the ring and hold it flat
x: The interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, exactly the angle of sp² carbons, so benzene's ring is planar (with parallel p orbitals above and below it). Cyclohexane's sp³ carbons need about 109.5°, which a flat hexagon cannot give, so its ring puckers.

q: In electrophilic substitution reactions, the benzene ring acts as:
o: An electron-poor species that is attacked by nucleophiles
An electron-rich species that is attacked by electrophiles
x: The delocalised π cloud makes benzene a source of electrons, so it is attacked by electron-seeking species (electrophiles) such as NO₂⁺ and Br⁺.

q: A hydrocarbon C₇H₈ adds 3 mol of H₂ on catalytic hydrogenation to give C₇H₁₄. It does not decolourise bromine water, and hot KMnO₄ oxidises it to benzoic acid. The hydrocarbon is:
x: An aromatic ring explains the three H₂ added without bromine water decolourising, and oxidation to C₆H₅COOH shows one side chain: C₆H₅CH₃. Cycloheptatriene is also C₇H₈ but its localised C=C bonds would decolourise bromine water.

q: According to the molecular orbital treatment, the delocalised π electron cloud of benzene is formed by:
o: Head-on overlap of sp² orbitals of adjacent carbons
Sideways overlap of six unhybridised 2p orbitals, one on each carbon
Overlap of carbon sp³ orbitals with hydrogen 1s orbitals
Sideways overlap of p orbitals in three separate, isolated pairs
x: Each carbon has one unhybridised 2p orbital; all six are parallel and overlap sideways all round the ring, forming one continuous π cloud. Head-on overlap of sp² orbitals gives the σ framework, not the π cloud.

q: The intermediate formed when an electrophile attacks the benzene ring is:
o: An arenium ion (a carbocation, also called a σ-complex)
x: The electrophile uses two π electrons to form a σ bond to one ring carbon, leaving a positive charge on the ring: the arenium ion. A carbanion would carry a negative charge.

q: Methylbenzene is treated with chlorine in bright sunlight at its boiling point, with no catalyst. The main monochloro product is:
x: Light and heat give free-radical substitution on the methyl side chain, producing C₆H₅CH₂Cl. With FeCl₃ in the dark, chlorine would instead substitute on the ring at the ortho and para positions.

q: In benzene, the unhybridised p orbital on each carbon atom is oriented:
o: Perpendicular to the plane of the ring
In the plane of the ring, pointing to its centre
x: The three sp² orbitals lie in the plane of the ring at 120°, so the leftover p orbital stands perpendicular to that plane. This lets all six p orbitals lie parallel and overlap sideways.

q: The rate-determining (slow) step in electrophilic substitution of benzene is:
o: Loss of H⁺ from the arenium ion
Attack of the electrophile on the ring to form the arenium ion
Combination of the lost H⁺ with a base
x: Forming the arenium ion breaks the aromatic π system, so it needs high activation energy and is slow. Loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity and is fast.

q: Which of the following groups is meta-directing in electrophilic substitution of benzene?
x: The nitro group withdraws electrons and directs incoming electrophiles to the meta position. –CH₃, –OH and –Cl are all ortho/para directors.

q: The H–C–C bond angle in benzene is:
x: Every carbon is sp² hybridised with a trigonal planar arrangement, so all bond angles in benzene are 120°. 109.5° is the tetrahedral angle of sp³ carbon.

q: In the arenium ion, the ring carbon bonded to both the electrophile and a hydrogen atom is hybridised as:
x: That carbon now forms four σ bonds (two ring C, one H, one electrophile) and has no p orbital in the π system, so it is sp³. The other five ring carbons remain sp².

q: Nitration of methylbenzene gives mainly:
x: The methyl group is an activating ortho/para director, so the nitro group enters mainly at the 2- and 4-positions (o- and p-nitrotoluene). The ring, not the side chain, is nitrated.

q: Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene is correct?
o: They are alternately long single and short double bonds
All six are the same length as the C=C bond in ethene
All six are equal in length, between a C–C single and a C=C double bond
All six are the same length as the C–C bond in ethane
x: Because the π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, all six C–C bonds are identical and of intermediate length (about 1.39 Å, between 1.54 Å and 1.34 Å). Alternating bonds would be expected only for a fixed Kekulé structure.

q: The arenium ion is less stable than benzene because:
o: It has more π electrons than benzene
Its delocalised π system no longer covers all six ring carbons
Its positive charge sits on one carbon only
It has lost a carbon atom from the ring
x: One ring carbon becomes sp³, so the remaining four π electrons are spread over only five carbons and aromatic stability is lost. The positive charge is in fact delocalised over three carbons, not one.

q: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene to cyclohexane is −120 kJ mol⁻¹. The measured enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. The resonance (delocalisation) energy of benzene is about:
x: A Kekulé structure with three fixed C=C bonds should release 3 × 120 = 360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene releases only 208 kJ mol⁻¹, so it is 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable. Subtracting one cyclohexene value (208 − 120 = 88) is the tempting slip.

q: How many σ bonds are present in one molecule of benzene, C₆H₆?
x: There are six C–C σ bonds round the ring and six C–H σ bonds, so 12. The π electrons are extra and delocalised. Counting only the ring bonds gives 6, and adding the three Kekulé π bonds to the ring bonds gives 9.

q: With bromine and FeBr₃, benzene gives bromobenzene and not an addition product such as C₆H₆Br₂. The main reason is that:
o: Benzene has no π electrons for bromine to attack
Addition would need an sp carbon in the ring
Substitution keeps the delocalised π system, while addition would destroy it and lose the resonance stabilisation
Bromobenzene is formed by free radicals, which cannot add to rings
x: After the arenium ion forms, losing H⁺ restores the full six-electron delocalised ring, which is much more stable than a product with isolated double bonds. Benzene does have π electrons (that is why electrophiles attack it), and the reaction is ionic, not radical.

q: 7.8 g of benzene is completely hydrogenated to cyclohexane over nickel at about 200 °C. What volume of hydrogen at STP is used? (C₆H₆ = 78 g mol⁻¹, molar volume 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹)
x: 7.8 ÷ 78 = 0.1 mol benzene. C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂, so 0.3 mol H₂ = 0.3 × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³. Forgetting the 1 : 3 ratio gives 2.24 dm³.

q: Chlorine is passed into boiling benzene in bright sunlight with no catalyst. The product formed is:
x: Under ultraviolet light and no halogen carrier, benzene adds three Cl₂ molecules by a free-radical path, giving 1,2,3,4,5,6-hexachlorocyclohexane (benzene hexachloride). Chlorobenzene needs a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeCl₃ or AlCl₃, the tempting slip; C₆H₅CH₂Cl comes from methylbenzene.

q: Only one 1,2-dibromobenzene is known. If benzene had only one Kekulé structure, with fixed alternating single and double bonds, how many 1,2-dibromobenzenes would be expected?
x: With fixed bonds, the two Br atoms on neighbouring carbons could be joined either by a C–C single bond or by a C=C double bond, giving two different compounds. Only one exists because all ring bonds are identical (resonance). Answering 3 confuses this with the three positional isomers (1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-).

q: In the nitration of benzene with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and concentrated H₂SO₄, the role of the sulphuric acid is to:
o: Supply the SO₃ electrophile that attacks the ring
Oxidise benzene to phenol before nitration
Protonate HNO₃, which then loses water to form the nitronium ion, NO₂⁺
Act as a solvent only, taking no part in the reaction
x: H₂SO₄ is the stronger acid: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. The NO₂⁺ ion is the electrophile. SO₃ is the electrophile in sulphonation, which needs fuming sulphuric acid, the tempting mix-up.

q: Benzene is warmed with chloroethane in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The organic product is:
x: This is Friedel–Crafts alkylation: AlCl₃ pulls Cl from chloroethane, giving an ethyl electrophile that replaces one ring H, forming ethylbenzene and HCl. Chlorobenzene would need Cl₂, and C₆H₅COCH₃ is the acylation product with ethanoyl chloride.

q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The product is:
x: In Friedel–Crafts acylation, AlCl₃ forms the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺, which substitutes the ring to give the ketone C₆H₅COCH₃ (acetophenone). Ethylbenzene would need an alkyl halide; confusing acylation with alkylation is the common slip.

q: Benzene is heated with fuming sulphuric acid to form benzenesulphonic acid. The electrophile that attacks the ring is:
x: Fuming sulphuric acid contains dissolved SO₃; its sulphur carries a large partial positive charge and attacks the π electrons, giving C₆H₅SO₃H. SO₄²⁻ and HSO₄⁻ are negative ions and cannot act as electrophiles; NO₂⁺ is the nitration electrophile.

q: 39 g of benzene is nitrated and the yield of nitrobenzene is 80%. What mass of nitrobenzene is obtained? (C₆H₆ = 78, C₆H₅NO₂ = 123 g mol⁻¹)
x: 39 ÷ 78 = 0.5 mol benzene gives at most 0.5 mol nitrobenzene = 61.5 g (1 : 1). At 80% yield: 0.8 × 61.5 = 49.2 g. Stopping at the theoretical yield gives 61.5 g; taking 80% of the benzene mass gives 31.2 g.

q: In the chlorination of benzene with Cl₂ and anhydrous AlCl₃, the AlCl₃ acts by:
o: Donating electrons to benzene to make the ring more reactive
Splitting Cl₂ into two chlorine free radicals
Accepting a lone pair from chlorine as a Lewis acid, polarising Cl₂ so that a Cl⁺ electrophile is produced
Removing water formed in the reaction
x: Aluminium in AlCl₃ has an empty orbital; it forms Cl–Cl→AlCl₃, which gives Cl⁺ and AlCl₄⁻. At the end AlCl₄⁻ takes the H⁺ lost from the ring, giving HCl and regenerating AlCl₃. Free radicals are the sunlight path that gives addition, the tempting confusion.

q: Nitrobenzene is nitrated further with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. Compared with benzene, the reaction goes:
x: –NO₂ withdraws electrons from the ring, so it deactivates the ring (higher temperature is needed) and directs the incoming group to the meta position. Deactivating and meta-directing go together for –NO₂; choosing ortho/para mixes it up with activating groups such as –CH₃.

q: Which is the correct order of decreasing reactivity towards nitration?
x: –OH donates its lone pair into the ring strongly, –CH₃ donates weakly (+I effect), and –NO₂ withdraws electrons, so electron density and rate fall in that order. Phenol is nitrated even by dilute HNO₃, while nitrobenzene needs heating with the acid mixture. Putting methyl above hydroxy underrates the lone-pair effect.

q: A student wants to make 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene from benzene in two steps. The correct order is:
o: Brominate with Br₂/FeBr₃ first, then nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄
Brominate with Br₂ in sunlight first, then nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄
Nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄ first, then add Br₂ in sunlight
Nitrate with HNO₃/H₂SO₄ first, then brominate with Br₂/FeBr₃
x: The first group decides where the second goes. –NO₂ is meta-directing, so bromination of nitrobenzene puts Br at position 3. Bromine first would direct the nitro group ortho and para, giving 1-bromo-2- and 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene, the tempting wrong order. Bromine in sunlight adds to the ring instead of substituting.

q: Chlorobenzene is nitrated with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. The main products are:
x: Halogens are a special case: they withdraw electrons by the inductive effect (the ring reacts more slowly than benzene) but their lone pairs direct the electrophile to the ortho and para positions. Linking deactivation with meta direction, true for –NO₂, gives the tempting 3-isomer; the C–Cl bond is not replaced.

q: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, is heated with alkaline KMnO₄ and the mixture is then acidified. The organic product is:
x: Hot permanganate attacks the side chain at the carbon next to the ring and oxidises the whole chain, whatever its length, down to one –COOH on the ring; the extra carbon is lost as CO₂. Keeping both side-chain carbons gives the tempting phenylethanoic acid; the ring itself is not oxidised or reduced.

q: Methylbenzene is first oxidised with hot alkaline KMnO₄ (then acidified), and the product is nitrated with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. The main final product is:
x: Oxidation turns –CH₃ into –COOH, giving benzoic acid. –COOH withdraws electrons and is meta-directing, so nitration gives 3-nitrobenzoic acid. Using the ortho/para direction of the original –CH₃ group gives the 2- and 4-isomers, the tempting slip from ignoring the order of steps.
